Find pattern p (length m) inside text s (length n). Brute force restarts after each mismatch: O(nm). KMP never moves backwards in s. It precomputes, for every prefix p[1..i], nxt[i] = the length of its longest border (前缀函数 / 失配数组): a proper prefix that is also a suffix.
On a mismatch after j matched characters, the last nxt[j] characters of s still match the first nxt[j] of p, so set j = nxt[j] and try again; no character of s is read twice. Total O(n + m).
ABABABC ABA
ababacababaca ababaca

Both loops are the same code: building nxt is "searching p in itself". The while-loop looks slow, but j rises by at most 1 per step and every fallback lowers it, so the total work is O(n + m) (P3375).

Use p[j + 1] with 1-based strings and remember j = nxt[j] after a full match, otherwise overlapping matches (ABA in ABABA) are lost. Compare j with m, not with the string's size after adding the padding space.

C C LANGUAGE · ADDITIONAL INFORMATION In C the strings are char arrays read with scanf("%s", s + 1) so that s[1] is the first letter, and the length is strlen(s + 1) . The two loops are identical. C++ string with a leading space gives the same 1-based layout.

title: What nxt tells you about periods

text: cabcabca
aaaaa

If a string has a border of length b, shifting it by n − b lines it up with itself, so n − b is a period. The longest border nxt[n] gives the shortest period n − nxt[n] (P4391: "cabcabca" is a cut of "cab" repeated).
The string is an exact repetition of its shortest period only when n % (n − nxt[n]) == 0. Following nxt[n], nxt[nxt[n]], … lists every border from longest to shortest.
babababa
The shortest non-empty border is the last stop on the chain i → nxt[i] → nxt[nxt[i]] → …. Walking the chain each time can be slow, so store it: shortest[i] copies shortest[nxt[i]] (P3435).
Counting borders with extra conditions (P2375 动物园 : borders no longer than half) also walks the nxt chain, with a second pointer that never grows past i / 2.
Tries for words and prefixes; the 0-1 trie for maximum xor.
a b c d d words: a, b, ad, acd green = a word ends here
A trie (字典树) stores a set of strings as paths from the root, one edge per letter.
Words with a common prefix share the start of their path. Node numbers are handed out as needed: ch[u][c] is the child of u along letter c, 0 if missing.

Insert and look-up both walk the word letter by letter: O(length), independent of how many words are stored. Mark the node where a word ends, otherwise "ad" would wrongly count "a" as present when only "ad" was inserted.
a b c ad acd
a a e
OK REPEAT WRONG

The array size is the total number of letters inserted plus one, not the number of words. Each node keeps whatever the problem needs: an end mark, a counter, a "visited" state (P2580). set<string> would also work here, but the trie also answers prefix questions.
i int intern internet in integer internal

Prefix questions are natural on a trie: the words that are prefixes of w are exactly the word-ends on w's path. The longest chain "each word is a prefix of the next" ends at some word, and has as many words as there are word-ends on its path: i → in → int → intern → internet (P1481).
Count in the other direction too: store how many words pass through each node, and "how many words start with this prefix" is one look-up (P2922 Secret Message uses both counts).
bit 2
bit 1
bit 0
want 0
want 1
want 0
go the opposite way at each bit, from the highest

Write numbers in binary from the highest bit and insert them into a trie with two letters, 0 and 1. To find the stored y that makes x xor y largest, walk from the top bit and take the opposite bit whenever that child exists: a 1 in a higher bit beats everything below it.
Insert all numbers, then query each one: the largest xor of a pair in O(n · 31). The greedy is right because bit k is worth more than bits 0 … k − 1 together.

The xor of the path u → v equals dis[u] xor dis[v], where dis is the xor from the root: the shared part above their meeting point cancels (x xor x = 0). So "longest xor path in a tree" becomes "largest xor of two numbers" (P4551).

Size the 0-1 trie as (number of values) × (bits) + 1 nodes. A persistent 0-1 trie answers the same question inside a range of the array (P4735, P4592); the k largest pair xors use a heap on top (P5283).

Key points to memorise
1. Border: a proper prefix that is also a suffix. nxt[i] = longest border of p[1..i].
2. Build nxt and search with the same loop: while mismatch, j = nxt[j]; if match, j++.
3. After a full match set j = nxt[j] to find overlapping matches. O(n + m).
4. Shortest period = n − nxt[n]; a full repetition only if it divides n.
5. All borders: nxt[n], nxt[nxt[n]], … down to 0.
6. Trie: ch[u][c], nodes = total letters + 1; mark word ends.
7. Prefixes of w = word-ends on w's path; words starting with w = pass count at w's node.
8. 0-1 trie: insert bits from high to low; for max xor take the opposite bit when possible.
9. Tree path xor = dis[u] xor dis[v].
